dimensions.label: Cheapest way to get a live, sellable store
dimensions.a: $39/mo (Basic) — one plan, hosting and checkout included
dimensions.b: About $25/mo — the plugin is $0 plus budget hosting

dimensions.label: Who handles hosting, backups and security updates
dimensions.a: Shopify — bundled into every plan, nothing to set up
dimensions.b: You, or whichever host you hire — it's a plugin, not a hosted service

dimensions.label: Extra fee for using a payment gateway other than the platform's own
dimensions.a: 2% (Basic), 1% (Grow) or 0.6% (Advanced) on top of the gateway's rate
dimensions.b: None — 0% platform fee no matter which gateway you use

dimensions.label: Staff accounts on the cheapest plan
dimensions.a: None — Basic is the owner only; a second login means moving to Grow
dimensions.b: Unlimited — WordPress user roles cost nothing extra

dimensions.label: Product and order limits
dimensions.a: None — unlimited products on every paid plan
dimensions.b: None — unlimited products and orders on the free core plugin

dimensions.label: Selling in person with a point-of-sale system
dimensions.a: Built in on every plan; POS Pro adds advanced tools at $89 per location a month
dimensions.b: Not built in — needs a separate POS extension and card reader

dimensions.label: Changing how the storefront or checkout code works
dimensions.a: Limited to Shopify's themes, apps and Liquid templates
dimensions.b: Full — it's open-source PHP running on your own server

dimensions.label: Time and skill needed to launch
dimensions.a: Sign up, pick a theme, add products — live the same day, no code
dimensions.b: Needs a working WordPress site first, then the plugin, a theme and a host

dimensions.label: Moving your store to a different host later
dimensions.a: Not possible — a Shopify store only runs on Shopify's own servers
dimensions.b: Yes — it's your WordPress database; move it to any host without rebuilding

verdicts.why: Shopify is the simpler default with no WordPress skills on hand; pick WooCommerce instead only if you already run WordPress or have someone who can maintain it.
An agency already comfortable with WordPress gets full code control across client builds and avoids paying a per-store subscription for every site it launches.
A course or coaching business needs cohort, drip-content and community tools, not a product-catalog checkout; both platforms are built around shipping goods.
A booking-and-invoice business needs scheduling software, not a storefront; only add one of these if you also ship a real product catalog.
Most freelancers selling a handful of digital products need a lighter checkout tool, not a full ecommerce platform built for inventory and shipping.
A software company needs recurring billing built into its own app, which is a different job than either platform's product-catalog checkout.
